articles.title: How Auction Guarantees Work
articles.card: Many top lots have a buyer lined up before the sale. How guarantees and irrevocable bids work, and why critics worry.
articles.summary: At the big evening sales in New York and London, many of the most expensive lots already have a buyer lined up before the bidding starts. That promise is called a guarantee. This is how guarantees work, who pays for them, and why parts of the trade are uneasy about them.
articles.description: How auction guarantees and irrevocable bids work, who backs them, how they are disclosed, and why some in the art trade see them as a risk.
articles.body:
The basic deal

A guarantee is a promise to the seller of a minimum price. The figure is agreed privately and is not published. In the simplest version, if the work fails to sell, the auction house pays the seller the agreed sum and keeps the work. In return the house expects a bigger share of the sale, either a higher seller's commission or a cut of any price above the guarantee.

For the seller this removes the risk of a public failure. For the auction house it is a way of winning the consignment against a rival. If the work sells well, the house and any backer share in the profit, though the seller may have to give away some of the upside. If it does not sell, the house owns a work it has already paid for.

Sharing the risk with outside backers

Most big guarantees are now shared with outside backers. Christie's calls the arrangement a third-party guarantee. Sotheby's introduced its own version, the irrevocable bid, in 2009. The Art Newspaper described the two in 2018 as essentially the same thing.

The backer agrees in advance to bid up to a set level. If someone else bids more, the backer is paid for having taken the risk. According to Artnet News, that payment can be a set fee, a share of the amount above the guarantee, or both. If nobody bids more, the backer buys the work. A backer who wins can also pay less than other bidders would have, because the fee is subtracted from the final price.

The share of the upside is a matter for negotiation. The Art Newspaper put a typical figure at 20% to 30% of the amount above the guarantee in 2018, with deals ranging from 10% to 50%. In 2025, insiders quoted by Apollo put it at 15% to 20%.

Backers can also win the lot they guaranteed, and that can come with a discount. Mari-Claudia Jiménez, co-head of the art law practice at Withers and a former Sotheby's chair, told Apollo that "Christie's pioneered the idea that if you were the guarantor you would always get a discount." Artnet News reported that when a first printing of the US Constitution sold at Sotheby's in November 2021, Sotheby's had found an irrevocable bidder at the last minute: the hedge fund manager Kenneth Griffin, who won the lot. The price was first given as $47.4m with fees and later revised down to $43.2m, and Artnet concluded that Griffin had received a $4.2m discount. As Artnet explains, auction houses "legally have to report net prices whenever the buyer receives a financing fee".

How buyers can tell

Guaranteed lots are marked, though the marks vary between houses and have changed over time. In 2011 The Art Newspaper listed the symbols then in use. Christie's used a circle for its own guarantee, and both a circle and a diamond for a lot backed by a third party. Sotheby's used a horseshoe for an irrevocable bid, and an underlined v to show that someone with an interest in the lot might be bidding. In 2025 Apollo described a Canaletto at Christie's in London whose online listing carried a diamond, showing a third-party guarantee.

Christie's relies on announcements instead. Jennifer Zatorski, then its international commercial director, told The Art Newspaper in 2011: "Announcements are made that someone with a financial interest will be bidding." Now that catalogues are mostly online, Citi points out, buyers have to listen to the list of lots the auctioneer reads at the start of the sale. Even that list does not say whether a third party is paying a reduced buyer's premium.

The rules have been tested. Christie's has cited New York City law, which says an auctioneer's interest in a lot, "direct or indirect", must be disclosed. In 2015 The Art Newspaper reported that at least five works in Christie's New York sale on 13 May had outside backers that the catalogue did not show. Christie's first left those works off a list it supplied, then said they were "subject to an in-house guarantee, as noted in the catalogue", and that it had met its legal obligations. The lawyer Frank Lord of Herrick Feinstein told the paper: "It would seem like the auction house would have to disclose that."

A short history

How long guarantees have existed is, in Apollo's words, "a matter of debate". Philip Hook, a former director of Impressionist and modern art at Sotheby's, says the house guaranteed £35,000 for Poussin's The Adoration of the Shepherds in 1956 and lost £6,000 on it. The Art Newspaper, citing an unnamed source, dates the first guarantees to 1971, when Sotheby's offered a group of Kandinskys and other works from the Guggenheim with a guaranteed minimum. Apollo says guarantees stayed rare until the art market boom of the early 2000s.

The most expensive early lesson came from Phillips. Bernard Arnault bought the house in 1999 and used large guarantees to compete. The Art Newspaper says the 2001 Smooke sale carried a guarantee of over $180m and raised $86m. Apollo gives $85m against a rumoured $170m. Arnault sold the firm in 2002 (Apollo says a majority stake) after losses of about $400m.

The boom that followed ran on guarantees. According to Noah Horowitz's book Art of the Deal, cited by The Art Newspaper, Sotheby's issued $902m of guarantees in 2007, up from $131m in 2005. When the market turned, some deals went badly wrong. Apollo cites a Wall Street Journal estimate that by the end of 2008 Christie's and Sotheby's held about $63m of art they had been obliged to buy. Guarantees all but disappeared between 2008 and 2010.

They came back with the market. Before Christie's New York sale in May 2015, 50 of the 85 works were marked as guaranteed, 36 by the house and 14 by third parties. In May 2018 Modigliani's Nu couché sold at Sotheby's New York for $157.2m (The Art Newspaper does not say whether that figure includes fees). The Nahmad family had reportedly given it the highest third-party guarantee then on record, at $150m.

How common they are now

Guarantees are concentrated at the very top of the market. Ben Gore, Christie's chief operating officer, told Apollo that only 1.5% of the house's lots carry a guarantee. By value the picture is different. Lindsay Dewar of the research firm ArtTactic told Apollo that nearly 73% of lots by hammer value in the post-war and contemporary evening sales at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips were guaranteed in the first half of 2025. Apollo gives 72% for Impressionist and modern art. Artnet News, citing ArtTactic, reported that guaranteed lots made up 83% of the total value of the November 2021 New York sales, a record.

A fully guaranteed sale does not mean strong bidding. At the Emily Fisher Landau sale at Sotheby's in November 2023, all 31 evening lots were guaranteed, and Apollo says 13 of them sold at or below the low estimate. Insiders told Apollo that margins at the top of the market can be as low as 2%.

The arguments for and against

Supporters say guarantees do what they claim to do: protect the seller. The dealer Helly Nahmad told The Art Newspaper in 2011 that guarantees "are like an insurance". Artnet News takes the comparison a step further: "If the auction guarantee is the insurance for the consignor, the irrevocable bid is the insurance for the auction house." In 2018 Adam Chinn, then Sotheby's chief operating officer, said: "I don't think there's a conflict of interest."

Critics worry about what bidders cannot see. In the same 2018 article, Harry Smith of the art advisory firm Gurr Johns said: "Guarantees have the potential to be the next big art-market scandal". The lawyer Rebecca Foden of Boodle Hatfield said they "distort the market and inflate prices". The economist Olav Velthuis, speaking in 2015 about the push for openness, said "you want more transparency—but this is resulting in the opposite." Felix Salmon, chief financial correspondent at Axios, has described heavily guaranteed auctions as "more like gussied-up private sales".

What it means

For anyone reading auction results, a guarantee changes what the hammer price tells you. When most of a sale's value was guaranteed, much of the result was agreed in private before the auction began. A lot that sells at or near its guarantee, possibly to its own backer at a net price, says less about demand than a lot that several people competed for. The symbols and the auctioneer's opening announcements are the only public clues, which is why they are worth paying attention to.

articles.title: New York November 2026 Auctions: Collections, Guarantees and a Van Gogh Record
articles.card: A Van Gogh record, a Kandinsky record, and a week built on private collections and guaranteed lots.
articles.summary: New York's November sales were carried by private collections, guarantees and a handful of very expensive pictures. A Van Gogh set a new record for the artist after a last-minute settlement over its wartime history.
articles.description: The main results of the New York November 2026 evening sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips, with hammer and with-fees prices, and what the week shows about the top of the market.
articles.body:
Twice a year, in May and November, the big auction houses hold their most important sales in New York. Before this autumn's round, The Art Newspaper expected Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams to bring at least $2.04 billion between them. Below are the main evening sales of 16 to 18 November, as reported by The Art Newspaper. We have not checked each figure against the houses' own lot pages. Prices are given as the hammer price first and then with the buyer's premium, the way the reports give them.

Sotheby's, 16 November

Sotheby's opened the week with two sales: its Now and Contemporary evening auction and the collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum. Together they made $378.7 million with fees.

  • The Baum collection sold every one of its 24 lots, for $90.8 million hammer ($109.9 million with fees). A third of them sold below the low estimate.
  • Yayoi Kusama's No. 3P.B. (1960) made $12.5 million hammer, $15 million with fees, a record for the artist.
  • The top lot was Roy Lichtenstein's Reflections on "Painter and Model" (1990), at $22 million hammer ($24.6 million with fees).

Sotheby's said works from single owners made up almost 60% of the evening's total.

Christie's, 17 November

Christie's 20th-century evening sale made $521 million hammer and $627 million with fees, at the low end of its estimate. Of 75 lots offered, 36 were guaranteed before the sale, 31 of them by outside backers. Six lots did not sell and three were withdrawn.

  • Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1923) made $74 million hammer ($85.8 million with fees), a record for the artist. The seller had bought it at Sotheby's in 1986 for $1 million.
  • Gustav Klimt's Litzlbergkeller (1915–16) made $71 million hammer ($82.3 million with fees).
  • The artist Jeff Koons was among the sellers. Works from his collection made $104.7 million with fees, led by Picasso's Le Baiser (1969) at $26.5 million hammer, well below its $40 million low estimate. Koons had bought it in 2008 for $17.4 million.

Christie's auctioneer Adrien Meyer described "a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace".

Phillips, 17 November

Phillips' modern and contemporary evening sale made $85.75 million hammer, $104.4 million with fees, up 55% on the same sale a year earlier. Fourteen of its 22 lots were guaranteed. Amedeo Modigliani's limestone Tête (1911–12) made $38.2 million hammer ($44.6 million with fees). Phillips' chairman Robert Manley said nearly 90% of the works offered had never been sold at auction before.

Sotheby's, 18 November

The biggest night was Sotheby's sale of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection from Argentina, followed by its Modern evening sale. Together they made $663.3 million hammer, $777.8 million with fees.

Vincent van Gogh's Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890) sold to the dealer William Acquavella for $165 million hammer, $190.4 million with fees. The artist's previous auction record was $117 million with fees, set in 2022. The day before the sale, Sotheby's announced a settlement between the sellers and the heirs of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, after questions about the painting's history during the Nazi era.

The 12-lot collection as a whole made $412 million with fees against an estimate of about $450 million, with half the lots selling below their low estimates. In the Modern sale that followed, Aaron Douglas's Harriet Tubman (1931) made $12 million hammer ($14.48 million with fees) against an estimate of $2.5 million to $3.5 million, a record for the artist. Mary Cassatt also set a record, at $11 million hammer ($13.3 million with fees) for Summertime (1894–95).

What the week shows

Three patterns stand out from the reports.

  • Collections drive the sales. Single-owner collections, from the Baums to the Blaquier-Arrietas and Koons, supplied many of the top lots, including the Van Gogh.
  • Guarantees are everywhere. At Christie's nearly half the lots were guaranteed, and at Phillips almost two thirds. A guaranteed lot sells whatever happens in the room, so high sell-through rates say less about demand than they seem to.
  • Estimates were not always met. Picasso's Le Baiser sold well below its low estimate, and half of the Blaquier-Arrieta lots sold below theirs. Others did better: the Kandinsky sold within its estimate and the Modigliani above it. The totals were large, but buyers did not chase every work.

As the Art Basel and UBS report showed for 2025, growth at auction is concentrated in the most expensive works. One week in New York tells you about that top tier. It says little about the market for most artists.

articles.title: Auction Houses Raise Buyer's Premiums in 2026
articles.card: Sotheby's, Phillips, Christie's and Bonhams all changed their fees this year. Here is what a buyer now pays.
articles.summary: Four of the biggest international auction houses changed what buyers pay in 2026. In each case the top rate on the first part of the price went up.
articles.description: Sotheby's, Phillips, Christie's and Bonhams all changed their buyer's premium rates in 2026. What changed, when, and what it means for buyers and sellers.
articles.body:
When a lot sells at auction, the buyer pays the hammer price plus a fee to the auction house, the buyer's premium. The premium is charged in bands: a higher rate on the first part of the price and lower rates above set thresholds. In 2026 Sotheby's, Phillips, Christie's and Bonhams all changed those rates or bands. Here is what changed and when.

Sotheby's, from 13 February

Sotheby's was first. From 13 February 2026 its lowest rate rose from 27% to 28%, and the band it applies to became much wider, The Art Newspaper reported. In London, 28% now applies up to £1.5 million, where 27% used to stop at £800,000. In New York the threshold moved from $1 million to $2 million. The 22% band now runs to £6 million or $8 million, and 15% applies above that, as before.

The Antiques Trade Gazette worked through an example. On a hammer price of £1.5 million, the premium rises from £370,000 to £420,000. The new rates apply across Sotheby's salerooms and categories, except wine and spirits. A Sotheby's spokesperson declined to comment to The Art Newspaper.

Phillips, from 12 April

Phillips announced a new structure for all auctions held on or after 12 April 2026, in New York, London, Hong Kong and Geneva. According to a summary by the law firm Grossman LLP, the rates are 29% up to $2 million, 22% from $2 million to $8 million and 15% above.

Phillips also offers lower rates through what it calls priority bidding. A bidder who leaves a binding written bid at least 48 hours before a live sale, at or above the low estimate, pays a reduced premium if they win. The chief executive, Martin Wilson, said the aim was to encourage early bidding and give sellers more certainty. When the scheme was first announced in 2025, the adviser Todd Levin told Artnet News that bidders should not be penalised for bidding in the room.

Christie's, from September

When Sotheby's made its change, a Christie's spokesperson told the Antiques Trade Gazette that the house had no plans to change its rates. By September it had. Christie's now charges 28% on the first $2 million of the hammer price in New York, 22% up to $8 million and 15% above, MyArtBroker reported. In London the 28% rate applies up to £1.5 million, under a schedule effective from 1 September 2026 in Christie's buying guide. The previous rates, set in September 2025, were 27% up to $1.5 million or £1 million, according to The Art Newspaper.

Bonhams, from 1 October

Bonhams wrote to clients in early September, in a letter published by ArtDependence. For sales after 1 October 2026 the rates are:

  • 30% on the first £25,000 of the hammer price (previously 28%)
  • 28% from £25,001 to £500,000
  • 25% from £500,001 to £1 million
  • 21% from £1,000,001 to £5 million
  • 14% above £5 million

Bonhams said its costs had risen considerably since its last change in July 2023, and that rates on higher-value property had come down. Wine, coins and medals, and motor cars and motorcycles are excluded, as is arms and armour in the US. ArtDependence reported no change to the fee charged to sellers.

What it means for buyers and sellers

For a buyer, the practical effect is that the same hammer price now costs more at lower and middle price levels. At 28%, a £100,000 hammer price costs £128,000 before any tax on the premium. That is why it matters, when comparing results, whether a price is quoted as the hammer or with fees.

Some in the trade argue that sellers end up paying too. MyArtBroker's report quotes the adviser Josh Baer, who says collectors know the total they will spend and will not bid beyond it, so a higher premium means a lower hammer price. MyArtBroker sells art privately and competes with auction houses, so its view is not neutral.

For more on how the premium changes what a result means, see our feature on auction results and emerging artists.

articles.title: What It Costs a Gallery to Show at an Art Fair
articles.card: Stand prices at Frieze and Art Basel, the bills that come on top, and why small galleries carry the most risk.
articles.summary: Art fairs now bring in a large share of what many galleries sell. They are also expensive, and the price of the stand is only part of the bill.
articles.description: What galleries pay to show at art fairs, from stand prices at Frieze and Art Basel to shipping, travel and staff, and why small galleries carry the most risk.
articles.body:
Why galleries go

The number of fairs has grown quickly. Citing the 2015 TEFAF art market report, Artnet News says there were 55 fairs worldwide in 2000 and at least 180 by 2014. Writing in February 2026, Tim Schneider wrote that there are now "hundreds of fairs per year".

For dealers, fairs are where much of the selling happens. The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026 found that art fair sales made up 35% of dealer turnover in 2025. Dealers surveyed by Artnet News said they make "between 20 and 60 percent of their annual sales" at fairs.

The stand

The big fairs such as Art Basel and Frieze charge by the square metre. Many fairs do not publish their prices, so the best figures come from reporting. In 2018 The Art Newspaper compared estimated prices for a 40 sq m stand in the main section of several fairs. At Fine Arts Paris the estimate was $60,840, all included. At Art Basel Hong Kong it was $34,400 and at Art Fair Philippines $7,600. The cheapest booth at Independent New York was $10,000. The paper noted that many fairs would not give figures, while Tefaf publishes its costs.

More recent prices show how fairs now charge different rates for different stands. At Frieze London in 2025, the main section cost £582 per sq m for stands of 30 to 50 sq m, rising to £658 for the largest stands of 110 to 130 sq m. In 2021 there had been a flat rate of £524. Frieze Masters charged £732 per sq m for every stand, up from £631 in 2021. The Focus section for younger galleries went the other way, from £338 per sq m in 2021 to £276, so a 30 sq m Focus stand cost £8,280 in 2025 against £9,390 a year earlier.

Art Basel's prices are in Swiss francs. When it introduced its new Premiere section in 2025, The Art Newspaper reported that a 32 sq m stand there cost SFr22,000, against almost SFr26,000 for the same size in the main section. A 30 sq m stand in Statements, the section for younger galleries, cost SFr10,000.

Everything else

The stand is far from the only cost. In a survey of dealers, Artnet News found that taking part in Art Basel Miami Beach cost galleries between $120,000 and more than $275,000 once shipping, furniture hire and dinners were included. The main-section booth alone was $50,400 to $100,800, depending on size. Airfare and shipping together "can run around $50,000", and Artnet says these costs are similar whatever the size of the gallery.

Artnet set out two galleries' own estimates. A small gallery with five to ten staff put its costs at $75,000 on the booth, $8,000 on extras, $20,000 on flights and hotels, $15,000 on shipping and $10,000 on entertaining, a total of $128,000, against gross sales of about $2m. A mid-sized to large gallery with 25 to 35 staff put its total at $275,000, with $100,000 for the booth, against gross sales of about $5m. Short-term insurance costs smaller galleries proportionally more, and they may need to hire temporary staff.

Gross sales are not profit. Galleries share the sale price with their artists, and an even split remains common, though it is not a fixed rule. If the small gallery above kept half of its $2m, it would have about $1m before paying the $128,000 fair bill and all its other costs. That is our own illustration, not a figure Artnet reported.

Who loses money

Dealers in the Artnet survey said they failed to make a profit at a fair between 15% and 50% of the time. Olav Velthuis of the University of Amsterdam told Artnet: "People don't realize that fairs are loss leaders for many small galleries." Magda Sawon of Postmasters gallery put the problem plainly: "the ones that make tons of money at fairs are paying the same to participate as those that lose money."

Costs are still rising. The Art Basel and UBS report found that dealers' operating costs rose by about 5% in 2025, faster than the 2% rise in their sales. Dealers surveyed for the previous year's report ranked fairs as their third most concerning cost, Tim Schneider wrote in February 2026. In 2025 The Art Newspaper reported that a dealer who sold nothing in Statements at Art Basel could leave "out of pocket by as much as $20,000", and that a small gallery may turn over less than $200,000 a year. Rózsa Farkas, founder of the London gallery Arcadia Missa, said: "The fairs in the middle are riskier and riskier for galleries." The gallery Clearing chose to skip fairs that year and put on a group show in a rented villa instead.

How fairs have responded

In August 2018 Art Basel and Frieze both announced sliding scales, so that larger stands pay more per square metre. Art Basel's new rates, due to start at the Basel fair in 2019, were to run from CHF 760 per sq m for the smallest main-section stands to CHF 905 for the largest, replacing a flat CHF 830. The Statements fee was to fall from CHF 12,000 to CHF 10,000, and galleries moving up to the main sector would get 20% off in their first year and 10% in their second. Shipping and staff were not covered. The dealer Thaddaeus Ropac called the change "a good start".

Speaking at a London conference in 2018, Jagdip Jagpal, director of India Art Fair, said that supporting younger galleries was "not a charitable act… just good business sense." Frieze London introduced tiered prices in 2024, and sponsors now help some younger galleries: Stone Island has funded a bursary for Focus galleries since 2023, and Tiffany & Co. does the same for the Artist-to-Artist section from 2025. Kristell Chadé, Frieze's executive director of fairs, said the aim is to help galleries make "the step up into the main section." Art Basel's fair director Maike Cruse called the new Premiere section the "sweet spot" that had been missing between Statements and the main section.

What it means

A fair is a bet made in advance. Artnet describes it as paying hundreds of thousands of dollars up front with no guarantee of a payoff. In Artnet's two examples the fair bill came to a similar share of gross sales, around 5% to 6%, but a small gallery has much less room for a bad week. Artnet notes that a small gallery could sell out and still barely recoup its costs.

Dealers still go because a fair can bring more than sales. The San Francisco dealer Anthony Meier told Artnet that the value of a fair "could be on the sell side, the buy side, a referral, or an introduction to an artist." Freddie Powell of Ginny on Frederick put the case for taking the risk: "Yes, every fair is a risk, but if my gallery can't take risks now, when can we?"

articles.title: The Art Market in 2025: What the Art Basel and UBS Report Found
articles.card: Sales rose 4% to $59.6 billion. The growth came from the top, while mid-sized dealers and online sales shrank.
articles.summary: Global art sales grew in 2025 for the first time in three years. The growth came mostly from the most expensive works, and dealer sales barely moved.
articles.description: Global art sales rose 4% to $59.6 billion in 2025, according to the Art Basel and UBS report. The growth sat at the top of the market, while mid-sized dealers and online sales shrank.
articles.body:
Each spring, Art Basel and UBS publish an estimate of how much art changed hands the year before. The report is written by the cultural economist Clare McAndrew of Arts Economics, and the 2026 edition, the tenth, came out on 12 March 2026. It is also built partly from surveys of dealers, so its numbers are estimates and should be read that way.

This report sets out what it found about 2025, and what the figures do and do not show.

The headline

Sales of art and antiques by dealers and auction houses came to an estimated $59.6 billion in 2025, up 4% on 2024. The number of transactions rose 2% to about 41.5 million.

That ends two years of falling sales, but it is not a return to the peak. Artlyst, summarising the report, puts the 2022 total at $68.1 billion.

Where the money went

The report splits sales between dealers and auction houses.

  • Dealers, including galleries, sold an estimated $34.8 billion, up 2%.
  • Public auctions made $20.7 billion, up 9%.
  • Private sales by auction houses, the deals they broker outside the saleroom, came to just under $4.2 billion, down 5%.

So auctions grew faster than galleries, and within auctions the growth sat at the top. At public auction, the value of lots over $1 million rose 21% and lots over $10 million rose 30%. Below $50,000, both value and volume fell 2%. All ten of the year's most expensive lots sold in New York. The most expensive was Gustav Klimt's Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, which made about $236 million at Sotheby's.

Tastes at the top also moved back in time. By value, Impressionist and Post-Impressionist sales at auction rose 47% and Old Masters 30%. Contemporary art, which the report defines as work by artists born after 1945, was flat at $1.4 billion. This fits what we described in our feature on auction results for emerging artists: buyers have been retreating from the newest names towards established ones.

Three markets dominate

The United States, the United Kingdom and China together accounted for 76% of sales by value, the same as the year before.

  • United States: 44% of the market, with sales up 5% to $26.0 billion.
  • United Kingdom: 18%, up 2% to $10.5 billion. Public auctions grew, while dealer sales were subdued.
  • China: 14%, with sales up just over 1% to $8.5 billion. Auctions in mainland China strengthened and Hong Kong weakened.
  • France: 8%, up 9% to $4.5 billion, and the largest market in the EU.

Elsewhere the picture was mixed. Switzerland and Austria each grew 13%, while Germany fell 10% and Italy 2%.

A hard year for the middle

The report's dealer survey covered more than 1,650 galleries and dealers in 70 markets, according to Artlyst. It shows a trade that grew on paper while costs rose faster.

Dealers' operating costs went up by about 5% on average, more than their sales. More dealers said profitability had fallen (38%) than said it had improved (33%).

Results depended heavily on size. Dealers turning over less than $500,000 saw double-digit growth in average sales, and those above $10 million grew 3%. Dealers turning over between $1 million and $10 million saw sales fall by 1%. That squeeze on mid-sized galleries is discussed in our feature on how galleries build careers.

Dealers also saw fewer buyers. The average number of individual buyers per dealer fell to 57, the lowest since 2021, and for the smallest dealers it fell 40% to 29. Almost half of buyers (49%) were new to the dealer they bought from.

Art fairs became more important. They accounted for 35% of dealer sales, up from 31% in 2024 and the highest share since 2022.

Online sales shrank

Sales made online fell to $9.2 billion, the lowest since 2019. Online-only sales were 15% of the market, against a peak of 25% in 2020. Online sales still matter for new buyers and lower prices, but the highest-priced lots were sold in live sales.

Women artists

Women made up 45% of the artists represented by dealers, up from 35% in 2018. Their share of dealer sales by value was 37%, up from 28% in 2018. At galleries working in the primary market, women were half of the artists and 44% of sales by value. The gap has narrowed, but it has not closed.

What dealers expect for 2026

Dealers were more hopeful than a year earlier. 43% expected sales to improve in 2026, up 10 points on the year before, and 19% expected them to fall. Among mid-sized auction houses, 21% expected weaker sales, down from 40% a year before.

Reading the figures

The report is useful, but three limits are worth keeping in mind.

  • Dealer figures come from surveys. Galleries do not publish their sales. The dealer figures are estimates based on an annual survey of dealers. The auction figures draw on sales data from auction houses and data providers.
  • A total hides the spread. A 4% rise driven by a small number of very expensive lots says little about the market most artists and buyers deal with. Below $50,000, auction sales fell.
  • One year is not a trend. 2025 was better than 2024, but sales remain below 2022. Whether the recovery holds depends on what happens next.

articles.title: Why Luxury Brands Work With Artists
articles.card: From Murakami and Kusama at Louis Vuitton to the Prada foundation: what brands and artists each get from the deal.
articles.summary: Louis Vuitton has worked with artists on its products for more than twenty years, and other houses have done the same. The terms are private, and what each side gets out of the deals is only partly known.
articles.description: Why luxury brands such as Louis Vuitton and Prada work with artists, what the brands and the artists each get from it, and the criticism the deals attract.
articles.body:
Murakami and the monogram

One of the best-known partnerships began in 2003, when the designer Marc Jacobs and Louis Vuitton launched a product collaboration with the Japanese artist Takashi Murakami. His reworkings of the monogram ran until 2007, according to The Business of Fashion, though other accounts give later end dates. The same article says Vuitton's work with artists helped turn "a staid French luggage label" into "one of the most valuable fashion brands in the world", and that Murakami "helped to cement Vuitton's new image."

Not everyone in the art world was comfortable. When Murakami's retrospective at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles included Vuitton bags for sale, the former auctioneer Simon de Pury recalls, it "made the soi-disant defenders of high art cringe." Vuitton and Murakami worked together again in 2024, two decades after the first pairing.

Other artists followed. Richard Prince worked with the house in 2008, according to nss magazine. In 2017 Jeff Koons reworked masterpieces by Leonardo, Rubens, Fragonard, Gauguin and others for Vuitton's Neverfull, Speedy and Keepall bags. De Pury's verdict: "It was a brand splashing brands on a brand."

Kusama, the largest of them all

In summer 2012 Louis Vuitton launched a collection with Yayoi Kusama that The Business of Fashion called "probably the largest artist collaboration initiated by any luxury goods or fashion house to date." It covered leather goods, clothing, shoes, sunglasses, watches and jewellery. Window displays ran in 460 Louis Vuitton stores in 64 countries, and BoF says the Kusama windows and concept store at Selfridges in London were "the largest single brand takeover the store has ever engaged in."

The deal sat alongside museum work. Vuitton supported Kusama's retrospective at Tate Modern, which BoF says was visited by 186,551 people, and sponsored its tour to the Whitney in New York. The deals were brokered by Glenn Scott Wright, director of the Victoria Miro gallery, working closely with Kusama's Tokyo gallery, Ota Fine Arts. He described two separate contracts, one for the windows and one for the design collaboration with Marc Jacobs.

A second Kusama collaboration followed in January 2023, offering 400 objects. Writing in The Art Newspaper, Georgina Adam wrote that Kusama's "latest works are just a tired reiteration of all that has gone before". She noted that Kusama, then 93, did not seem to have commented on the collaboration herself, and asked who exactly was signing on the "(polka) dotted line". None of the reporting we read answers that question.

What the brands get

For a brand, the attraction is the association. An article in The Conversation notes that "studies have suggested that an association with art allows commercial brands to be perceived as more luxurious", though it does not name the studies. The partnerships also bring attention: BoF reports that during the Kusama launch, the press said Selfridges' concept store repeatedly sold out of pieces.

Sales figures are harder to find. None of the sources we checked gives reliable numbers for the Kusama or Koons lines. A 2017 nss magazine feature says Murakami's line made "above $ 300 million profit only in the first year", but it does not say where the figure came from, so it should be treated with caution.

What the artists get

None of the sources we read says how much any artist was paid. What is on record is exposure. BoF says Kusama appeared on the covers of magazines including Wallpaper, Pop and The Saturday Telegraph Magazine. Glenn Scott Wright says the collaboration "made her into an international household name", and de Pury says it "helped towards establishing her in the art-world firmament."

There are risks too, especially for younger artists. Hervé Mikaeloff, an art consultant to LVMH and the Fondation Louis Vuitton, told BoF: "We have to be careful, particularly with a young artist, that it doesn't affect their career."

Foundations and museums

Some houses have gone further than collaborations and built institutions of their own. Prada opened Fondazione Prada in 1993, and its touring Prada Mode programme brought exhibitions by Damien Hirst to Dubai in 2022 and by Theaster Gates to Abu Dhabi in 2025. The Conversation describes Fondazione Prada and the Fondation Louis Vuitton in Paris as "fully-fledged art galleries", with collections that include Jeff Koons at Prada and Matisse and Warhol at Vuitton. The Vuitton foundation's building was designed by Frank Gehry.

Smaller collaborations are common across the industry. Longchamp worked with Tracey Emin in 2004, Dior's Lady Dior Art project invites artists to reinterpret its best-known handbag, and Gucci has replaced some of its campaigns with digital paintings by Ignasi Monreal and murals by Alex Merry.

What it means

The case for these partnerships is clearest from the brand's side, where the link with art can make a product seem more luxurious. For artists the picture is less clear. The exposure can be large, as Kusama's case shows, but the terms are not made public, and the artist's name ends up on handbags as well as in museums. The Conversation's view is blunt: "it is hard to see that these forays into the art world are about anything more than merely enhancing their own brand."

articles.title: How Galleries Build Long-Term Artist Careers
articles.card: Pricing, placement and patience, and why the galleries that carry artists through mid-career are under the most strain.
articles.summary: A gallery's job is often described as selling art. The harder part is deciding what not to sell, to whom, and how quickly.
articles.description: How galleries use pricing, placement and time to build artist careers, and why rising costs and early signings by the largest galleries are putting that model under pressure.
articles.body:
When a gallery agrees to represent an artist, very little is exchanged at first. No money changes hands up front, and many galleries work from a consignment agreement for the works they hold instead of a full contract. What begins is a working arrangement that both sides expect to last for years, and in the best cases for decades. Sadie Coles, who opened her London gallery in 1997, has represented Sarah Lucas and John Currin for almost 30 years.

That length of time is the point. A single sold-out exhibition proves that there is demand this season. A career is something else: steady prices, work in public collections, and buyers who are still there when fashion moves on. This article looks at how galleries try to build the second thing, and why it has become harder to do.

What the commission pays for

The usual arrangement is consignment. The artist lends work to the gallery, the gallery sells it, and the two share the price. An even split remains common, though it is a convention and not a fixed rule. Discounts and tax normally come off the top before the money is divided.

In return the gallery carries the costs of selling: the space, the staff, the opening, the shipping, the fairs. Those costs are rising. The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026 found that dealers' operating costs rose by about 5% on average in 2025, while total dealer sales rose 2% to $34.8 billion. Art fairs alone accounted for 35% of dealer turnover.

The work has also widened. Coles describes representation today as "much more multilayered" than it was. It can include managing an artist's archive, producing digital material and overseeing production, which she says can run from small pieces to very big ones. Stefan Benchoam of Proyectos Ultravioleta in Guatemala City says his gallery is the first point of contact for visiting curators from biennials and major museums.

Pricing slowly

The first tool a gallery has is price, and the long-term approach is to use it sparingly. Prices are set by where an artist is in their career and what comparable work has sold for, with the aim of steady progression over time.

The reason for caution is that art prices are hard to reverse. A 2025 Artnet News report quotes the Zurich adviser Thomas Stauffer: "Once prices are too high, it's nearly impossible to walk them back." In the same report the dealer Sebastian Gladstone says he keeps prices conservative and is more interested in an artist's fourth or fifth exhibition than the first.

That discipline is under strain. The same report says the price ceiling for work described as "emerging" has moved from about $10,000 to roughly $30,000 to $45,000.

Placement: choosing the buyer

The second tool is choosing who buys. In most markets the highest offer wins. In the primary art market, dealers often prefer the buyer who will do most for the artist's standing.

The writer Tim Schneider calls this a matching market, where seller and buyer both have to agree. In an excerpt from his book The Great Reframing, he gives the example of a gallerist choosing a $75,000 sale to the Guggenheim over a $200,000 sale to an unknown buyer. The museum sale pays less today. It adds a line to the artist's record that supports every later price.

Waiting lists come from the same thinking. Schneider writes that the New York dealer Mary Boone is widely credited with making them standard gallery practice in the 1980s, though she may not have invented them. He notes that a collector's standing often counts for more than their place in the queue. Some consignment agreements allow a shared 20% discount for museums, because a public collection means long-term care and the chance of exhibition.

Why the model is under pressure

All of this is slow, and it costs money before it earns any. That is manageable only if the gallery is still representing the artist when the work pays off.

Often it is not. Smaller galleries have complained for more than a decade that larger ones sign their artists once sales begin. The Art Newspaper reported in 2013 that the growth of the largest galleries was squeezing smaller operators. The 2025 Artnet report describes the next stage: the biggest galleries now sign artists much earlier, so the traditional climb from small gallery to large one is being compressed. Pam Evelyn joined Pace in 2023 at the age of 27. Sasha Gordon joined David Zwirner in September 2024.

The figures show where the strain falls. In 2025, dealers turning over less than $500,000 saw double-digit growth in average sales, and those above $10 million grew 3%. Dealers in the middle, with turnover between $1 million and $10 million, fell by 1%. They were the only group whose average sales went down.

Shared representation

One response is for galleries to share artists. In November 2023 Hauser & Wirth began partnering with younger and smaller galleries to represent emerging artists together. The stated benefit is that the artist can keep working at a comfortable scale and the smaller gallery stays in business.

Not everyone is convinced. One dealer quoted in the Artnet report describes "a lot of confusion now about who's doing what and why", and the report notes that smaller galleries can lose leverage. Others are changing how they work with artists directly. The London gallerist Rose Easton holds regular check-ins with her artists about their sales and about how the gallery itself is doing. She says younger artists are asking why galleries are expected to take 50%.

What it means

For an artist, the useful question about a gallery is less how quickly it can sell and more what it turns down: which prices, which buyers, which opportunities that arrive too early. For a collector, a gallery that prices carefully and places work with institutions is doing the things that tend to hold value.

For the industry, the open question is who pays for the slow years. Linda Pyke, a director at THK Gallery in Cape Town, says the relationship between a gallery and an artist needs decades to mature. The 2025 figures suggest that the galleries in the middle, too big to grow like the smallest dealers and too small to compete with the largest, are finding that wait hardest to pay for.

articles.title: What Auction Results Mean for Emerging Artists
articles.card: Hammer prices, fees, resale royalties and the boom and bust of 2021 to 2024: how to read a young artist's auction record.
articles.summary: A strong auction price looks like good news for a young artist. It is often the least reliable number in their career, and they rarely see any of the money.
articles.description: What an auction result does and does not tell you about an emerging artist: hammer price and fees, who receives the money, the Artist's Resale Right, and how to read a result.
articles.body:
Most of what an emerging artist's work sells for is private. Galleries rarely publish prices, and private sales between collectors are not reported. The exception is auction. When a work sells at auction, the result is published and logged in price databases, where it stays.

That makes auction results the figures everyone quotes. It also makes them easy to misread. This article sets out what an auction result does and does not tell you about an artist at the start of their career.

Which number are you looking at?

An auction produces more than one price. The hammer price is the winning bid. The buyer then pays a fee on top, the buyer's premium, which goes to the auction house and not to the seller.

The premium is large enough to change the picture. Each house sets its own rates, usually in bands that fall as the price rises. Three examples in sterling show the range. Bonhams charges 30% on the first £25,000 of the hammer price for sales after 1 October 2026. Christie's charges 28% up to £1.5 million under a schedule effective from 1 September 2026. Tate Ward's terms for buyers set 25% plus VAT on the hammer price up to £500,000, and 12% plus VAT on any part above that.

Taking 25% as an example, a work that hammers at £10,000 costs the buyer £12,500, before any tax due on the premium.

Published results often include the premium, so it is worth checking which figure a report is using. The seller receives less than the lower one, because the house also takes a commission from them. When two results are compared, the first thing to check is whether both are quoted the same way.

Who gets the money

Almost never the artist. A work at auction is being sold by someone who already owns it. In a report on quick resales, Artnet News found that artists and their galleries rarely gain directly when a work is resold. Voluntary payments from sellers do happen, but they are uncommon.

In the UK there is one legal exception. Under the Artist's Resale Right, an artist is owed a royalty when a work is resold through an auction house or dealer for £1,000 or more. The rate is 4% on the portion up to £50,000 and falls in steps above that, with a cap of £12,500 on any one sale. It is collected and paid out by collecting societies such as DACS.

So a painting resold for £10,000 earns its maker £400. That is real money for an artist early in their career, but it is a small share of the price. The United States has no equivalent: Artnet reports that federal resale royalty bills have failed at least eight times since 1978.

What a high price does next

A record result can affect more than one sale. Owners of similar work learn what it might fetch, and buyers who could not get work from the gallery can try the saleroom instead.

The scale of this in recent years was unusual. Auction sales of works by artists born after 1974, offered at auction within three years of being made, rose from $22.8 million in 2012 to $257.4 million in 2021, according to Artnet.

Then it reversed. The research firm ArtTactic found that the auction market for artists under 40 fell 43% in 2023 and a further 53% in the first half of 2024, as reported by Anny Shaw in The Art Newspaper. The paper gave examples. Flora Yukhnovich's auction sales fell 88% in 2023 against the year before, and Njideka Akunyili Crosby's fell 72%, Salman Toor's 68% and Avery Singer's 63%. Artnet, which defines the category differently, recorded a 31.3% fall in the first half of 2025, against a fall of 8.8% for fine art auctions overall.

The paintings did not get worse between 2021 and 2023. The number of people bidding for them changed. An auction price measures demand in one room on one day, and for a young artist with few works in circulation, two determined bidders are enough to set a record.

Why galleries worry

The concern for galleries is what happens to their own prices. During the boom, some raised their primary prices after inflated auction results. One collector quoted by The Art Newspaper called those increases unsustainable.

This is why galleries try to keep new work out of the saleroom. Sale contracts that restrict resale have become standard, Anna Brady reported in The Art Newspaper in 2023. Typical terms bar resale for three to five years or give the gallery first refusal.

Whether those clauses would stand up is uncertain. Lawyers quoted in the same report disagree, and the adviser Sibylle Rochat notes that they have not been tested in UK courts. In practice galleries rely on something simpler: a blacklist. A buyer who resells too soon risks losing access to the gallery for good.

How to read a result

For anyone looking at an emerging artist's auction record, a few questions do most of the work.

  • Hammer or with fees? Compare like with like.
  • How does it sit against the estimate? A result far above estimate can mean strong demand, or a cautious estimate.
  • How many results are there? One sale is an event. A pattern over several years is information.
  • How old was the work? A piece resold within a year or two of leaving the studio says more about speculation than about lasting demand.
  • What else is on the record? Museum collections, a consistent gallery and steady exhibitions tell you more about a career than any single price.

Auction results are the most visible numbers in the art market, and for established artists with long sales histories they are useful. For artists at the start, they are best read as one piece of evidence among several, and usually not the strongest one.

articles.title: The Business Case for Art in Luxury Hospitality
articles.card: Hotels spend heavily on art. The evidence that it lifts room rates is thinner than the claims made for it.
articles.summary: Luxury hotels now talk about art the way they once talked about thread counts. The spending is real. The evidence that it pays is thinner than the enthusiasm suggests.
articles.description: How luxury hotels acquire and use art, what hotels, artists and galleries gain, and how much of the business case for art in hospitality has actually been measured.
articles.body:
In London, The Dorchester has spent two years restoring a suite designed in 1952 by the stage designer Oliver Messel, murals and all. Its rate on reopening was set at £15,000 a night, Claire Wrathall reported in The Art Newspaper. Across town a penthouse at Claridge's holds 75 works by Damien Hirst.

These are not isolated gestures. Wrathall notes that 757 five-star-plus rooms were expected in London in 2025 alone. With that many new luxury rooms competing for guests, art is one way for a hotel to stand out. This article looks at how hotels use it, who gains, and how much of the business case has been measured.

An old arrangement

Hotels and artists have traded with each other for a long time. From the 1930s, artists such as Matisse and Picasso traded works for stays at La Colombe d'Or in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, Maïa Morgensztern wrote for Artnet News. In 1992 Benesse House opened on the Japanese island of Naoshima as a museum and hotel in one building, a model Art Basel's Mahoro Seward treats as a starting point for the modern art hotel.

The commercial version arrived with Soho House, founded in 1995. Morgensztern reports that it set aside £150,000 to £400,000 for art at each venue, bought mostly from emerging artists for £1,000 to £5,000 a work, and often paid in stays, meals and memberships instead of cash.

The relationship has since moved upmarket. In 2018 the owners of the gallery Hauser & Wirth opened their own hotel, the Fife Arms in the Scottish Highlands, which holds about 16,000 works of art and design.

Three ways hotels get their art

The owner's collection. The simplest route is to hang what the owner already has. Seward lists several hotels built around a private collection, from Marrakech to Athens. It gives the collection an audience.

A partnership with a gallery. Here the gallery supplies the work and the hotel supplies the walls and the guests. Morgensztern found that galleries usually pay for production and installation, and that leading hotels rarely take a share of any sale. For one exhibition at a Paris hotel in 2019, about half of the buyers came through the hotel and half were existing clients of the galleries.

Commissions and licences. Larger groups need art in hundreds of rooms. One answer is to license reproductions. When the Archer hotel opened in New York in 2014, about half of the art budget went to the artists whose images were used, according to the adviser Deborah Goodman Davis, as Rachel Corbett reported in The Art Newspaper. The photographer Thomas Allen said in the same report that his own commission was "not all that much".

What hotels say they get

Three reasons come up most often.

The first is distinction. Seward argues that as luxury shifts towards experiences, art helps a hotel stand apart and gives guests a way into the local scene.

The second is attention. Joshua Gardner, who runs Broadwick Soho in London, told Wrathall plainly that "these days you need something for Instagram".

The third is price, and here the evidence weakens. In a 2017 CoStar report, the head of one art agency said he saw a direct link between a hotel's art strategy and the rates it can charge. In the same article a senior Wyndham executive, Brian Watson, admitted there is no formal science behind it.

How good is the evidence?

That admission is worth dwelling on. The figures quoted in favour of hotel art often come from the people who sell it.

One statistic in the trade press says that 80% of respondents believe the softer benefits of art feed through to revenue and room rates. It comes from a survey by NINE dot ARTS, an art consulting firm that works on hotel and property developments, and it records what property professionals believe, not what a hotel earned.

We did not find an independent study that isolates the effect of an art programme on a hotel's rates or occupancy. That does not mean there is no effect. It means the case currently rests on judgement and example more than on measurement.

What it means for artists and galleries

For artists the appeal is exposure to people with money and time. Morgensztern cites Alice Gray Stites, who looks after the art for the C21 Museum Hotels group. She bought a work by Titus Kaphar for about $25,000, and his work now sells for six-figure sums.

There are costs to weigh as well. Payment in kind is not income. A reproduction licence may pay little once an adviser and a gallery have taken their shares. And some artists dislike the setting. Morgensztern recalls that in 1959 Mark Rothko withdrew from a commission for a New York restaurant, reportedly because he did not want his paintings to be something diners glanced at.

For galleries a hotel can work as a second showroom. In the Paris example, half the buyers came through the hotel. The collector Kenny Schachter told Morgensztern that hotels are putting more interesting work on their walls but have not yet worked out how to sell it.

Questions worth asking

  • For hotels: What is the art for: distinction, press, or sales? Each needs a different programme and a different budget.
  • For artists: Is the fee paid in money? Who owns the image rights? Will the work be shown as art, with a label and a name, or as furnishing?
  • For galleries: Who pays for installation and insurance, and who keeps the buyer's details?

articles.title: How Public Art Activations Generate Attention
articles.card: From Banksy's London animals to the Fourth Plinth: what public art does for attention, and how far to trust the figures.
articles.summary: Art in a public place can draw a crowd that no gallery could hold. Working out what that attention is worth, and to whom, is harder than the headline numbers suggest.
articles.description: How public art draws attention, from civic commissions and sculpture trails to sponsored murals, how far the visitor and economic figures can be trusted, and what it means for artists.
articles.body:
In August 2024 a new work by Banksy appeared somewhere in London every day for nine days. A goat on a wall in the west, elephants in Chelsea, a gorilla lifting the entrance gate at London Zoo. Fans learned of each one through the artist's own website and Instagram account, the Associated Press reported.

Fans rushed to see each one. So did other people. A wolf painted on a satellite dish was carried off by masked men. A cat on a billboard was taken down by contractors while onlookers booed. The zoo put its mural behind an acrylic shield, watched by three security guards. One specialist told the AP that the public reaction might itself be part of the work.

The series was covered by news outlets around the world, the AP among them. Marketers call this kind of thing an activation. This article looks at how it works when the plan is deliberate.

Four kinds of public art event

The word covers several different things, and they have different owners.

The civic commission. A public body pays for a work in a prominent place. A well-known British example is the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square, where a new sculpture is installed every two years. The current work, Lady in Blue by Tschabalala Self, was unveiled in September 2026 as the 16th commission. The programme is funded by the Mayor of London with support from Arts Council England and Bloomberg Philanthropies.

The spectacle. A single large work, shown briefly. In February 2005 Christo and Jeanne-Claude placed 7,503 fabric gates along the paths of Central Park in New York for 16 days. More than four million people came, according to the Central Park Conservancy. The artists had first proposed it in the 1970s.

The trail. Dozens of decorated sculptures are placed around a town for a few months, then auctioned for charity. In Brighton and Hove, a trail of painted dog sculptures drew more than 350,000 visitors and raised £310,000 for Martlets Hospice in autumn 2016, organisers reported.

The sponsored wall. A brand or property developer pays an artist to paint a mural. This is the kind most argued over, as discussed below.

Why it works

The examples share a few features, and they are worth separating from the art itself.

  • It is free and in the way. Nobody has to decide to visit. The audience is whoever is passing.
  • It ends. Sixteen days, a few months, or until someone removes it. A deadline gives people a reason to go now.
  • It photographs. Each visitor's picture is another small advertisement.
  • It can be argued about. Online, people debated what the London animals meant for days, the AP noted.

How good are the numbers?

Public art events come with impressive figures attached. They deserve a closer look.

The Central Park Conservancy credits The Gates with an estimated $254 million in economic activity for New York. Its anniversary press release does not say who calculated that figure or how.

The Brighton trail was credited with adding £10 million to the local economy, along with 14.6 million social media impressions. Those statistics were commissioned by Wild in Art, which organised the trail with the hospice.

That does not make them wrong. But visitor counts for a free outdoor event are estimates, and an economic impact figure depends on assumptions about what people would otherwise have spent. Two academics who studied sculpture trails, John Thompson and John Day, wrote in the journal Local Economy that various claims are made about the economic, social and artistic impact of such trails, and that some people walk or drive past the exhibits without ever seeing them.

A fair reading is that public art reliably produces attention, and that the conversion of attention into money is much less well measured.

When a brand is paying

The sponsored mural raises a different question: is it art or an advertisement?

At least one city has drawn a legal line. Los Angeles adopted rules in 2013 banning commercial messages in murals, and in 2014 a mural carrying a beer logo was removed for breaching them, Christine MacDonald reported for In These Times.

Brands have adapted by leaving the logo off. MacDonald describes one mural paid for by a drinks company that carries no reference to it at all. The company promoted a film of the painting process instead.

Artists are divided. Some, MacDonald writes, worry that sponsored work blurs the line between art and advertising and makes it harder to find walls that have not been paid for. Others pointed out that corporate commissions pay far more than community mural grants, and artists need to earn a living.

What it means for an artist

Attention is not the same as income. Two of the London animals, the wolf and the cat, were taken down on the day they appeared, one by masked men and one by contractors.

For an artist offered a public commission, the practical questions are familiar ones.

  • Who is paying, and will the audience know?
  • How long will the work stay, and who decides when it goes?
  • Who owns it afterwards, and who may reproduce the image?
  • Is the fee for the work, or is the exposure being offered in place of one?

A public work can put an artist in front of far more people than a gallery exhibition. Whether that becomes a career depends on what happens next, and on the slower work described in our feature on how galleries build careers.

articles.title: Charity Auctions: Cultural Value and Commercial Considerations
articles.card: Charity sales raise large sums. Artists give the work, and the prices can distort an artist's record.
articles.summary: Charity auctions raise very large sums and almost nobody criticises them in public. The people who supply the art, and the people who rely on auction prices, have more mixed feelings.
articles.description: What charity art auctions are worth to charities, artists and buyers: the sums raised, what donating artists give up, how benefit results affect prices, and the Gift Aid rules.
articles.body:
The sums are not small. Sotheby's says its auctions raised more than $430 million for 240 charitable organisations in 2022, The Art Newspaper reported. Christie's put the figure for its own charity auctions at $440 million for the first half of that year alone, according to Melanie Gerlis in the same paper.

Much of it comes from big collections sold for philanthropy. Of Christie's first-half total, Gerlis noted, the Thomas and Doris Ammann collection brought $325 million, against $13.7 million from fundraising sales. Another part comes from a humbler source: living artists who are asked to give a work so that it can be sold for a cause. This article looks at what that exchange is worth to each side.

Why they work

A charity auction does something an ordinary appeal cannot. It offers the donor an object. The adviser Megan Fox Kelly told Gerlis that buyers are mostly chasing the art and not the cause, and that these sales draw money from people who might not otherwise give.

They also draw higher bids. Gerlis notes that buyers tend to pay more for charity lots, and that auction houses sometimes waive or reduce their fees. A small painting by Tracey Emin, And you Kissed me, made £80,000 at Bonhams's Cure3 exhibition for Parkinson's research. The report does not say whether that figure includes fees.

For the charity, then, the case is simple. The questions start with the people who provide the lots.

What the artist gives

An artist who donates a work gives up the income from it. They are also asked often. One artist interviewed for a 2018 report by Amy Costello estimated she received about 50 requests a year, and had paid for framing and shipping on works that then failed to sell.

Saying no is awkward. Anna Brady, writing in The Art Newspaper, wrote that picking holes in the charity auction model is "frankly, taboo", and that the buyer is usually celebrated while the artist is often forgotten. Dealers were often unhappy with the model because they were left out altogether, Robin Woodhead, formerly chief executive and chairman of Sotheby's International, told Brady.

The tax position can add to the sense of imbalance. In the United States, Costello reports, an artist who donates a work can deduct only the cost of materials, not what the work sells for.

What it does to prices

The commercial effects run in both directions, and both can cause trouble.

Too high. A charity room is generous by design. In 2008 the Red auction at Sotheby's, held for AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria charities, set 17 auction records for artists, Gerlis notes. Such records stay in the price databases. The fact that they were set at a benefit does not.

That matters because a single inflated result can start a run. Katya Kazakina of Artnet News describes the painter Jacob Kassay, whose work, estimated at $2,000 to $8,000, sold for $94,000 at a benefit. Speculators followed, the artist's auction record reached $317,000, and prices later fell sharply.

Too low. The opposite risk applies at smaller events. The Los Angeles gallery owner Mat Gleason told Costello that collectors use charity sales to buy for far less than a gallery would charge, which gives them less reason to pay full price elsewhere. That is one dealer's view, and the report offers no figures to test it.

Not every charity result enters the record. Kazakina notes that charity lots sold within the major houses' regular auctions are logged in price databases, while auctions run by charities themselves at galas are not.

What the buyer can claim

Buyers sometimes assume a charity purchase carries a tax benefit. In the UK the rules are narrow. Under HMRC's Gift Aid guidance, the buyer is paying for an item. Only the amount paid above the item's known retail value can count as a donation, and bidders must be told that value beforehand.

For something unique, the guidance treats the item's value as whatever it fetches in the auction. Buyers of original art should check with the charity before assuming any part of the price can be treated as a gift.

Models that share the proceeds

Some organisers have tried to rebalance the exchange. The Stand, an online platform launched in 2021 by Woodhead, gives 70% of each sale to the artist and their gallery, 20% to charity and keeps 10% for costs, Brady reported.

Sotheby's took a similar line with Artist's Choice in 2022. Artists and galleries consigned new work to auction, and 15% went to charity, a donation shared between the artist and the auction house. As we noted in our feature on primary and secondary markets, that format has not been repeated.

Questions worth asking

None of this is an argument against charity auctions. It is an argument for setting them up with care.

  • For artists: Is there a reserve, so the work cannot sell for a fraction of its gallery price? Will the gallery be involved? Will I be told who bought it?
  • For charities: Would a share of the proceeds for the artist bring better work, more often? Are estimates in line with gallery prices?
  • For buyers and anyone reading results: Was this price set at a benefit? If so, treat it as a measure of generosity as much as of value.

articles.title: How Artists Move Between Primary and Secondary Markets
articles.card: What happens when an artist's work reaches auction, and how galleries and auction houses now cross into each other's business.
articles.summary: The art market is usually described as two markets with a wall between them. In practice artists, galleries and auction houses cross it all the time, and each crossing changes who is in control.
articles.description: How artists and their work cross between the primary and secondary art markets: what galleries do when work reaches auction, artists who sell new work at auction, and how auction houses and dealers now overlap.
articles.body:
The textbook version is simple. In the primary market a work is sold for the first time, often consigned to a gallery directly by the artist. In the secondary market a work that someone already owns is sold again, usually through an auction house or a private dealer.

The two behave differently. Karim Crippa, writing for Art Basel, describes primary prices as moving gradually and under control, and secondary prices as driven by bidding and far more volatile. For an artist, the move from one to the other is the point where their prices stop being managed and start being public.

The usual direction

Most artists cross in one direction and do not choose when. A collector who bought from the gallery decides to sell, and consigns the work to auction. The artist is not the seller, so, as Crippa notes, the artist does not usually benefit from any jump in price.

Galleries prefer this to happen late. In a 2019 report for The Art Newspaper, Anna Brady quotes Marc Payot of Hauser & Wirth saying he would have preferred a work by Amy Sherald not to appear at auction yet, because there was still a lot of work to do on her institutional career.

The risk is a weak result. The adviser Lisa Schiff told Brady that an artist can sell well through galleries and still do badly at auction, and that this can leave them with no secondary market at all. Auction results are recorded in price databases such as Artnet's, so a poor one stays visible to every future buyer.

What galleries do when the work appears

Galleries do not simply watch. Brady's report describes several responses.

  • They are told in advance. The New York dealer Marianne Boesky says auction houses often let galleries know when their artists are in a sale.
  • They alert their collectors. One gallery director describes contacting clients who do not normally buy at auction when the estimate looks reasonable.
  • They hold their own prices. A work by Rashid Johnson had made $1.2 million with fees at Sotheby's, yet Hauser & Wirth offered his work at Art Basel for $475,000. Payot told Brady that one strong result is no reason to move gallery prices to that level.
  • They remember who sold. Alex Logsdail of Lisson Gallery says he would not sell again to a buyer who bought a work and put it into auction a year later.

Some go further. Jane Morris, writing in Apollo, notes that well-funded galleries have at times bid at auction to prevent a weak result. Boesky, for her part, says she does not want to hold up prices the market cannot sustain.

Is that kind of bidding allowed? The lawyer Jon Sharples, writing in The Art Newspaper, argues that a dealer acting alone to bid on work by their own artists is unlikely to break UK law, provided nobody is bidding on works they consigned themselves. Coordinated schemes to push up prices are a different matter and may be covered by the law on bid-rigging and fraud.

Going the other way

Occasionally an artist crosses on purpose, taking new work straight to auction.

The best-known case is from 2008, when Damien Hirst sold 223 new works at Sotheby's in London and bypassed his dealers. The two-day sale raised £111.4 million, Anny Shaw reported in The Art Newspaper.

Auction houses have since tried gentler versions that include the gallery. In September 2022 Sotheby's launched Artist's Choice, selling works consigned jointly by artists and their galleries. The six works in that first sale carried a combined estimate of $255,000 to $360,000 and made $919,800 with fees, according to Apollo.

The results were strong, but the idea has not spread. Shaw reported a year later that no further Artist's Choice sales had been held. A similar group of primary works offered at Christie's in the same month did less well, and Morris concludes that most living artists do not have the depth of demand an auction needs.

The houses become dealers, and the dealers become houses

The larger shift is quieter. Auction houses now do a great deal of selling away from the saleroom. Sotheby's reported $1.3 billion and Christie's $1.7 billion in private sales in 2021, Apollo notes. Those are negotiated deals at fixed prices, which is how galleries work.

Some of that is new work. Of the 14 private selling exhibitions Phillips held in 2022, eight featured primary-market works. In August 2023 Phillips also launched Dropshop, a channel for newly commissioned work under which artists receive 3% of resales made through the house.

Galleries cross the other way. Many sell secondary-market works alongside the artists they represent, and a resale handled by the gallery is one it can price and place itself.

What it means

For an artist, the two markets are less a pair of stages than a question of who is selling. When the gallery sells, the price is managed and the artist is paid. When a collector sells at auction, the price is public and the artist usually is not. In the UK the Artist's Resale Right returns a small share.

The experiments of the past few years are attempts to close that gap, by giving artists a seat at the auction or a cut of the resale. None has yet replaced the ordinary route. For most artists the move into the secondary market still happens when somebody else decides it should.
